nego.missiles.title: Missile Forces
nego.missiles.question: How far do you limit Iran's missile forces?
nego.missiles.o1d: Blocks new production only. Highly likely to be accepted.
nego.missiles.o2d: Cuts the stockpile with verification attached. A balanced demand.
nego.missiles.o3d: The hardest demand. You need enough leverage to back it.
nego.mines.title: Hormuz Mines
nego.mines.question: How are the mines in the strait to be handled?
nego.mines.o1d: Builds trust through a joint operation that includes Oman.
nego.mines.o2d: International monitors confirm clearance and any re-laying.
nego.mines.o3d: Demands the removal of every mine, including stored ones.
nego.sanctions.title: Economic Sanctions
nego.sanctions.question: How far do you adjust sanctions in exchange for the deal?
nego.sanctions.o1d: Eases sanctions in step with compliance to draw out an agreement.
nego.sanctions.o2d: Delays concessions, but lowers the chance Iran accepts.
nego.sanctions.o3d: More pressure, but a far higher risk of collapse.
nego.security.title: Security Guarantees
nego.security.question: What level of no-further-attack commitment do you offer?
nego.security.o1d: A commitment that neither side strikes first.
nego.security.o2d: Attacks stop only while verification holds.
nego.security.o3d: Keeps the military option, but raises the cost of the deal.

dev.heroTitle:
I wanted to command
the war that never ends.
dev.heroLead: Reading about what has actually happened around the Strait of Hormuz, I started wondering what it would feel like to sit in the president's chair and make three decisions every day. HORMUZ is that question, built through vibe coding with AI.
dev.threadsLink: Follow the build log on Threads
dev.stackTitle: A 3D strategy game that runs in a single browser tab
dev.stackLead: No install, no server. Open the link and it starts.
dev.stack1Body: Built with no framework. It runs in real time inside a 120,000-triangle budget, even on mobile browsers.
dev.stack2Body: You fight on the real coordinates and terrain of the Strait of Hormuz. If the connection drops, it falls back automatically to local terrain built from real coastline data.
dev.stack3Body: From the aircraft carrier down to the marine rifleman, each model is generated from a single image and then decimated to run on the web.
dev.stack4Body: The design docs, the code, the images and even the performance test harness were built in conversation with AI. You don't need to know much code — only the idea.
dev.aboutBody: You first choose the major branches of the past to set your starting figures, then make three National Security Council decisions each day. Choosing a military option drops you into a top-down RTS battle where you command the units yourself. The war can run to DAY 54, and negotiation opens on DAY 12.
dev.feature1: Six past-event decisions that set your starting figures
dev.feature2: Three decisions a day · Military · Diplomacy · Economy and Information
dev.feature3: Seven real-time 3D battles with five adaptive difficulty tiers
dev.feature4: Budget and congressional votes · Presidential override
dev.feature5: Ten endings driven by transit, oil, approval, international support and escalation
dev.noticeTitle: This is a fictional strategy simulation
dev.noticeBody: It is built on real place names and publicly reported events, but the events, figures and decisions in the game are fiction for education and entertainment. No real person's voice or frontal likeness is used, and civilian casualties are never a game objective.
